feed.title: Krunalkumar Shah — Blog
feed.subtitle: Articles by Krunalkumar Shah on mentorship, careers, cybersecurity research, and automation — practical writing drawn from real work.

entry.title: What a VPN Does and Does Not Do
entry.summary: A VPN is an encrypted tunnel to somebody else's server. That genuinely helps against a hostile network and an ISP that logs — but it moves who you have to trust rather than removing the need to trust anyone. What it does, the long list of what it does not, and the honest cases where it is the right tool.

entry.title: What Build Gates Taught Me About CI
entry.summary: Every gate in this site's build exists because something shipped broken and nobody noticed. Six of them, the bug behind each, and what they taught me about continuous integration — including the gate whose own regular expression was wrong, and which therefore blamed the fifty-two files that were correct.

entry.title: When a Static Site Outgrows Static
entry.summary: A static site can run compilers, an operating system emulator and a forensics suite entirely in the visitor's browser, so "static" is not a synonym for "simple". These are the honest signals that you have genuinely outgrown it, the intermediate steps most projects skip on the way to a backend, and the things you give up the moment you have a server.

entry.title: Why Every Number Here Is Counted
entry.summary: A number typed into a sentence is a claim with nobody responsible for it. It was true the day it was written and nothing since has had an opinion. This is why every figure on this site is recounted at deploy time instead — the mechanism, the real drift it was built to stop, and the honest limit on what counting can fix.

entry.title: Writing Comments That Survive
entry.summary: The comment that restates what the code does is the first one to go stale, because the code moves and the sentence does not. The comments that survive record something the code cannot say for itself: a measurement, an alternative that was rejected, a constraint that is load-bearing, and above all a bug that was actually hit. Examples throughout are from this site's own source.

entry.title: The First Week of an Automation Job
entry.summary: A day-by-day account of the first week of an automation engagement: the discovery conversation, the read-only access that always takes longer than the work, watching the process run once instead of being told about it, counting volume and error rate before anyone claims an improvement, and the steps that should be left alone or deleted rather than automated.

entry.title: How to brief a security consultant
entry.summary: Scope, environment, access, third parties, constraints and deliverable: what a security consultant needs from you before a quote can be honest, and the questions a good one will ask back.

entry.title: Read a Privacy Policy in Five Minutes
entry.summary: Privacy policies are reference documents laid out like essays, so reading them in order is the slowest way to get an answer. Here is the ordered method I use instead: what to search for, why the sharing section is the business model, what “as long as necessary” really means, and how to check a policy against the page it describes.

entry.title: The HubSpot Mistakes Hardest to Undo
entry.summary: Some CRM mistakes cost an afternoon and some cost a quarter. Object model, property sprawl, deal stages, lifecycle drift, duplicate records, imports with no key, and production changes with nowhere to be wrong — why each one resists repair, and the cheap prevention for each.

entry.title: Password advice that stopped being true
entry.summary: Composition rules, ninety-day expiry and blocked paste came from a 2003 NIST appendix whose author later said he regretted it. NIST SP 800-63B and the UK NCSC now advise against all three. What changed, why each rule failed mechanically, what is true instead, and what is still genuinely contested.

entry.title: AI agents, once you maintain one
entry.summary: Five different things get called an agent, and most products sold as one are a fixed chain or a router — usually the right choice. What changes once you maintain a real loop: evaluation sets instead of tests, a model dependency you cannot pin, caps on the loop, tool design, traces, and prompt injection.

entry.title: Your accounts after you die
entry.summary: Your accounts are secured against exactly the people who will need them. A practical guide to the legacy tools the platforms provide, password manager emergency access, backup codes and hardware keys, nomination in India, and the domain renewal that quietly takes everything else with it.

entry.title: What your browser tells every site
entry.summary: What a website reads about you before you click anything: the IP address, User-Agent and Accept-Language that arrive with the request, and the screen, time zone, CPU cores, GPU and canvas fingerprint a script reads afterwards. Why the combination identifies you when no single value does, why a fingerprint is harder to escape than a cookie, and why an unusual privacy setup can make you easier to pick out rather than harder.

entry.title: Why I quote fixed price
entry.summary: Why nearly every engagement I take ends up fixed-price: what it actually buys the client, the risk premium every fixed quote contains, why it punishes optimism and pushes towards defensive scoping, and the five kinds of work I refuse to price that way.

entry.title: Is “We Don’t Store Passwords” True?
entry.summary: Nearly every service says it never stores your password. It stores a hash, which is still password-derived data and still a cracking problem. The six rungs of what is actually stored, the signals that give a bad implementation away from outside, and the designs where the claim finally becomes true.

entry.title: Why Your Automation Broke, and How to Build One That Fails Loudly
entry.summary: A deprecated API version, a revoked refresh token, a renamed CRM field, a webhook delivered twice. The failure mode that matters is silence: a workflow that stops running produces no errors at all, which is why you alert on absence rather than on error.

entry.title: The Real Cost of a Manual Process
entry.summary: Minutes times frequency times a loaded hourly rate is where people start and stop, and it undercounts by a third before you reach rework, queue time and key-person risk. A method you can run on your own numbers today, including the cases where automating is the wrong call.

entry.title: How a SIM Swap Works, and Why an OTP Is Not the Protection You Think
entry.summary: Your number is a credential that a human at a retail counter can hand to somebody else. Why SMS was never an authentication channel, what the attacker does in the window, and the one tell worth knowing: a phone that drops to no service for no reason is an incident.

entry.title: What Consent Actually Means Under the DPDP Act
entry.summary: Free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, with clear affirmative action — which is why "by using this site you agree" is not consent. What a compliant notice looks like, what a Consent Manager is, and which parts still depend on Rules phasing in.

entry.title: Why Your Phone Feels Hacked, and Probably Is Not
entry.summary: The innocent explanations are usually right, and the "my phone listens to me" experience has a more interesting real answer than the myth. Then the signals that do warrant concern, the checks anyone can run, and honest safety advice on stalkerware.

entry.title: How to Read a Data Breach Notification
entry.summary: "We have no evidence of misuse" is absence of evidence. "Passwords were encrypted" usually means hashed, and the question is how. What the phrasing hides, and a checklist that differs by which data actually leaked.

entry.title: The Interview Questions I Ask
entry.summary: What each question is really testing, the signals that predict good engineers and the ones that only look like signal — and the interviewer failure modes that decide the next fifty minutes in the first five.

entry.title: The Mentee Mistakes That Cost the Most Time
entry.summary: Tutorial loops that feel like progress, starting over instead of finishing, asking for a roadmap instead of picking a problem. Each one with why it feels right, what it costs, and the specific different action.

entry.title: How to Read a Job Description
entry.summary: Requirements repeated in the responsibilities are real; the ones only in the bullet list often are not. What the familiar phrases carry, what is missing that should worry you, and how to test the description against reality on the call.

entry.title: What Deepfake Detection Can and Cannot Do
entry.summary: Every detector that returns a percentage is selling confidence it does not have, because the detector and the generator are the same arms race. What a forensic examiner actually looks at, and why the real defence against a cloned voice on a payment call is process rather than detection.

entry.title: UPI Fraud: How the Money Actually Leaves
entry.summary: A collect request and a payment look almost identical on screen, and one of them takes your money. The PIN authorises money leaving, always — no refund, cashback or prize has ever needed it. The scripts that reach people here, and what to do in the first hour.

entry.title: What Happens When You Click a Phishing Link
entry.summary: Opening the page, typing a password, approving an MFA prompt and running an attachment are four very different problems, and only some of them are serious. What the click itself discloses, why 2FA is not the reassurance people think, and an ordered checklist for the first thirty minutes.

entry.title: n8n, Make, or Zapier: An Honest Comparison
entry.summary: The decision that actually matters is not the feature list, it is where the workflow runs and whose infrastructure your client’s data crosses. Written from shipping production workflows in all three, including what happens when the vendor changes an API.

entry.title: What an Auditor Actually Wants From Security Training
entry.summary: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.3 asks for awareness, education and training, and an assessor asks to see who attended, what was covered and when. What counts as evidence, what does not, and why no trainer can promise an audit outcome.

entry.title: What a Security Review Actually Finds
entry.summary: The same findings recur: an ID in a URL nobody checks belongs to the caller, missing rate limits on reset flows, a secret in a build layer, a forgotten staging environment with production data. Why each happens, and why a clean review does not mean secure.

entry.title: Digital Arrest: The Scam That Keeps You on Camera
entry.summary: There is no such thing as a digital arrest — the anatomy of the fake-police video call, why acute stress makes careful people comply, and exactly what to do, including the conversation to have with an older parent first.

entry.title: Surface Web, Deep Web, and Dark Web: What the Three Layers Actually Are
entry.summary: The iceberg picture teaches three false things at once. The deep web is your inbox and your bank, the dark web is a small overlay network rather than a deeper layer, and "we found your data on the dark web" is doing far less than it sounds.

entry.title: Git, Explained From the Object Up
entry.summary: Git stops being spells the moment you know the three things any command can move. The object store, branching and rebase, the undo toolbox, and the reflog safety net — explained from the bottom, with receipts from rewriting 169 commits without changing a byte of content.

entry.title: What Sixty-Six Tiny Games Taught Me About Serious Software
entry.summary: The games page looks like a break from the serious work. It was the serious work in miniature: state machines, shared keyboards, saved dead ends and copy the code could not honour — every production bug class, caught small, with receipts.

entry.title: Scope the Work Before You Quote It
entry.summary: Most unprofitable projects were not underpriced, they were under-defined. The five questions to answer before you send a number, what belongs in writing, and how to handle a change of scope without either side feeling cheated.

entry.title: Passwords, Passkeys, and What Actually Protects You
entry.summary: Almost nobody loses an account to password guessing — they lose it to reuse, to phishing, or to a breach somewhere else entirely. What a passkey actually changes, what it honestly does not, and a practical setup worth an hour.

entry.title: Finding the Right Career When Everyone Has an Opinion
entry.summary: "Follow your passion" fails most of the people who try it. The three things that have to overlap, why testing beats deciding, the two-year rule, and which advice to ignore entirely.

entry.title: The Life of the Buddha, Without the Mythology
entry.summary: Who Siddhattha Gotama actually was, which of the famous episodes were added centuries later, what he taught across forty-five years of walking, and what he said about taking his word for any of it.

entry.title: Types of Love, and Choosing Someone to Marry
entry.summary: One English word does the work of a dozen different feelings. The kinds of love, how infatuation differs from the real thing, what research says predicts a marriage lasting, and the questions worth asking before you commit.

entry.title: What Happens After We Die
entry.summary: The oldest question, treated honestly: what each tradition actually claims, how the Hindu and Buddhist views genuinely differ from one another, what near-death research can and cannot establish, and living with an open answer.

entry.title: The Resume-Builder Paywall Trick
entry.summary: The editor is free until your entire work history is typed in — then the price appears at the download button. What happens to that data server-side, and why the browser's print dialog is the download button nobody charges for.

entry.title: What a Marriage Biodata Leaks
entry.summary: DOB, birthplace, mother's name, home address, income, and a photo that may carry GPS — one A4 page read the way an attacker reads it, and the sharing hygiene that costs nothing.

entry.title: How I Vibe Coded This Website — And the Mechanism That Made It Hold
entry.summary: I did not hand-write most of this site. What made it hold was the mechanism around the prompting — the prompt as a specification, the reasoning kept in the repository, adversarial review passes, and a build that refuses to publish damage.

entry.title: AI Driven, Human Assisted: The Default Just Inverted
entry.summary: Human driven, AI assisted was the safe arrangement for a decade, because the tool could not hold a plan. It can now — what the inversion changes, the four jobs a human keeps, and where AI driven is still the wrong default.

entry.title: Types of Cyberattacks, Mapped: Causes, Defenses, and the CIA Triad
entry.summary: Six attack families, what each one breaks, why they keep working, and the prevention and mitigation that actually help — one practical map built on the CIA triad.

entry.title: Security Compliance, Explained: GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOC 2, and More
entry.summary: A practical guide to security and privacy compliance — GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOX, ISO/IEC 27001, and SOC 2 — what each one is, who it binds, the requirements that matter, and how to tell which apply to you.

entry.title: India's IT Law, Explained: From the IT Act 2000 to the DPDP Era
entry.summary: A practitioner's map of India's IT law — the IT Act 2000, Sections 43 to 79, the struck-down 66A, the 2021 Rules, CERT-In directions, BNSS 94, and the DPDP Act.

entry.title: How Cybercrime Cases Are Solved: From First Alert to the Courtroom
entry.summary: How a cybercrime case actually gets solved — incident response, the police investigation, digital forensics, chain of custody, and what makes electronic evidence stand in an Indian court.

entry.title: Which AI Tool for Which Job: A Practitioner's Map
entry.summary: Chat, research, slides, images, video, meetings, code, automation — which AI tool fits each job, what the free tiers give you, and exactly where free stops.

entry.title: I Open-Sourced My AI SDR
entry.summary: CleverResponder is my open-source AI SDR for SmartLead and Instantly: it classifies replies, drafts with AI, gets Slack approval, sends, and follows up.

entry.title: Character Over Career: Five Choices I Live By
entry.summary: Character over career, satisfaction over success, failure over fear, people over place, goal over gossip — five choices that guide how I live and work.

entry.title: My Career Story: From Classroom to AI
entry.summary: From a $6 mentoring session to published security research, 5,000+ interviews, and AI pipelines — my honest career story, setbacks included.

entry.title: The Four M's Every Business Runs On
entry.summary: Manpower, money, mind, and management: what each pillar means, why businesses fail when one is missing, and how management binds the rest.

entry.title: Lessons from Running an Internship Cohort
entry.summary: Why small cohorts beat crowds, hiring for hunger over resumes, giving real work instead of exercises, and why mentorship is mostly restraint.

entry.title: How to Stand Out in an Internship Interview
entry.summary: Advice from 5,000+ interviews: why attitude beats aptitude, the homework nobody does, mistakes that sink candidates, and questions worth asking.

entry.title: Smart Feedback: How to Give and Receive It
entry.summary: Why vague praise fails, a three-part structure for feedback that actually helps, and how to receive criticism without getting defensive.

entry.title: How to Succeed in Software Development: The Four-Step Path
entry.summary: Make it work, make it modular, make it readable, then optimize. Why this order is the key to building software and automations that last.

entry.title: What Is a Fork Bomb in Linux?
entry.summary: How one line of Bash can freeze a hardened Linux system, why ulimit and blacklists fall short, and the smarter defense from my research.

entry.title: Automating Email Replies with n8n
entry.summary: How I build email reply automations with n8n: the five-stage workflow, where AI helps, guardrails that prevent bad sends, and mistakes to avoid.
